We have several ideas for changing the examples used in its post-training, the stage where an already trained model is taught how to respond.
We could remove a group of examples. We could replace them with different ones.
Each change sounds reasonable, but which one would actually help?

scenes.title: Looking back, or asking what if

lines.text: Finding examples associated with a bad answer does not automatically tell us which to remove to improve future answers.
One question looks back at how the model got here. The other asks what would happen if we changed something.
This is a research question, not a method we have already shown to work.
If a shortcut takes as much computation as trying every change directly, it has not helped us very much.
I don’t yet have evidence that we can make this decision more cheaply or more reliably than strong existing methods.
The work we have completed so far is narrower.
We built a tiny learner, to study how suppressing the learning contribution from one event changes its later behaviour.
One copy learns normally; in the other, that event’s contribution is suppressed.
Both then carry on learning.
Because these futures involve randomness, a comparison can be noisy.
Variance measures how much the comparison fluctuates between random runs.
Our pilot asked whether coordinating the random choices between the two copies could make the estimate more precise.
This is called coupling, an established idea.
Each copy still has to follow its own probabilities at every step.
We change how the choices are paired.
We checked 1,440 toy configurations with one- or two-step continuations.
We compared six baseline pairing methods with an oracle that could find the best allowed pairing in the tiny setup.
The condition for advancing to the planned longer-horizon test: at least a 20% reduction in variance against the best baseline, in at least one configuration from our chosen target family.
What did the oracle find?
The strongest result in that family was about 18.5%.
With full suppression of the event’s learning contribution, the strongest result was about 14.1%.
These were best cases, not averages, and they came from an oracle whose own computation was not a practical shortcut.
